notes: Ruling UNP placed in slot 1 (MD 2000 has it in 14). Template coalition slot 2 holds the Federal Party, which sat in Dudley Senanayake's national government from 1965 until it walked out over the shelved district councils; the actual remaining partner, Philip Gunawardena's MEP, is in 20. SLFP placed in 14 (non-aligned, has popularity) instead of MD's 18; LSSP in 18; CWC (ICFTU-leaning estate union) in 3. JVP placed in 5 (underground guerrilla movement in 1970) instead of MD's 4, which holds the pro-Moscow CP. Slot 23 is the Crown (Ceylon is a dominion until 1972) rather than MD's Nayakkar house.

0.name: Holdfast
0.text:
Holdfast was the codename of the coup planned for the night of 27 January 1962 by senior police and army officers, many from the Christian and Burgher elite, to remove Sirimavo Bandaranaike's government. Betrayed before it began, it ended in mass arrests and convictions, but in 1965 the Privy Council quashed the verdicts, and Colonel F. C. de Saram, C. C. Dissanayake and Douglas Liyanage are free men again.

Its men favour a firm, Western-aligned order: protection of the English-educated elite and the Christian schools, close ties with Britain and the United States, and no compromise with the Marxist parties. They have no organisation now, but their networks in the officer corps, the police and the Colombo clubs remain a reserve should the left come to power.

1.name: Eksath Jathika Pakshaya
1.text:
Founded in 1946 by D. S. Senanayake, the United National Party has led a national government since March 1965 under his son, Prime Minister Dudley Senanayake. J. R. Jayewardene, Minister of State and the party's chief strategist, is the strong man behind him; Philip Gunawardena's MEP still sits in the cabinet, while the Federal Party has walked out. A general election is due in 1970.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, a mixed economy open to foreign capital, the food drive for self-sufficiency in rice and friendly relations with the West within non-alignment. Its base is the propertied middle classes, low-country business and Kandyan landed families, much of the countryside and many minority voters, and the Lake House press gives it a powerful voice.

2.name: Ilankai Tamil Arasu Kachchi
2.text:
Known in English as the Federal Party, the Ilankai Tamil Arasu Kachchi has been the main voice of Ceylon Tamils since 1956. Founded in 1949 by S. J. V. Chelvanayakam, it joined Dudley Senanayake's national government in 1965 on the promise of district councils, then left the cabinet when the scheme was shelved. M. Tiruchelvam and A. Amirthalingam are among its leading figures.

It demands a federal constitution with an autonomous Tamil-speaking region in the north and east, parity of status for Tamil, an end to state-sponsored Sinhala colonisation of Tamil areas and citizenship for the plantation Tamils. Committed to nonviolence and parliamentary methods, liberal in outlook, it dominates the Jaffna peninsula and much of the east.

3.name: Ceylon Workers' Congress
3.text:
The Ceylon Workers' Congress is the largest trade union of Indian Tamil plantation workers and their political voice. Led by S. Thondaman, it organises hundreds of thousands of tea and rubber estate labourers in the hill country, most of whom were left stateless by the citizenship laws of 1948–49 and now face repatriation under the 1964 Sirima–Shastri Pact.

It fights for citizenship, wages, housing and union rights on the estates and bargains pragmatically with whichever government holds power, leaning towards the UNP and the Western free trade union movement. Its leverage lies in the plantations that earn most of Ceylon's foreign exchange: when the estates stop, the economy stops.

4.name: Lanka Kommunist Pakshaya
4.text:
The Moscow wing of the Communist Party of Ceylon, which kept the party's name when the pro-Peking faction broke away in 1963–64, is led by Pieter Keuneman and S. A. Wickremasinghe. Since 1968 it has been a partner of the SLFP and the LSSP in the United Front, whose common programme promises sweeping nationalisation.

It seeks a socialist Ceylon through parliamentary alliance and mass struggle, close friendship with the Soviet Union and state control of banks, plantations and foreign trade. Its strength lies in Colombo's unions, among educated Sinhala and Tamil radicals and in a disciplined cadre whose influence far exceeds its handful of seats.

5.name: Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna
5.text:
Founded in 1965 by Rohana Wijeweera, a former Lumumba University student who broke with the pro-Peking communists, the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna is a secret movement of rural Sinhala youth. Through its five lectures it recruits unemployed graduates, students and young villagers in the south, and the press has begun to call its followers Che Guevarists.

It denounces the old left as traitors to the revolution, attacks Indian expansionism and prepares in secret for an armed seizure of power. Its strength is the frustration of educated rural youth without jobs or prospects; its weakness is its inexperience and the attention it is beginning to draw from the police.

6.name: All Ceylon Buddhist Congress
6.text:
Founded in 1919, the All Ceylon Buddhist Congress is the leading lay Buddhist organisation of the island. Its 1956 report, The Betrayal of Buddhism, helped carry S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike to power, and its campaigns led to the state takeover of most denominational schools in 1960–61.

It demands that Buddhism be given the foremost place in national life, opposes Catholic Action and missionary influence, defends the poya holidays won in 1966 and Sinhala-medium education, and distrusts Western culture and capital. Its leverage is moral: it speaks for temple trustees, lay societies and monks across the Sinhala heartland, and no government can afford to ignore it.

7.name: Felix kandāyama
7.text:
Felix Dias Bandaranaike, a member of the Bandaranaike clan and Finance Minister in Sirimavo Bandaranaike's first government, leads the hard-nosed statist wing of the SLFP. Around him gather lawyers, party organisers and officials who want power used without apology, and who still resent the press barons whose campaign helped bring down the SLFP government in December 1964.

They believe in a strong executive armed with emergency powers, tight control of the press and the civil service, nationalisation of foreign firms and suspicion of Western capital. Their leverage is proximity to Sirimavo Bandaranaike and command of the party machine; in power they would make the state stronger than any rival.

8.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat
8.text:
Ceylon's Dawoodi Bohras are a close-knit Shia Ismaili trading community of Gujarati origin, prominent in the hardware and import trade of Colombo's Pettah. Their local congregations owe allegiance to the Da'i al-Mutlaq in Bombay, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin, who succeeded his father in 1965.

They are moderate, loyal and apolitical, seeking freedom of worship, protection of their mosques and trusts, and a business climate that does not choke private trade with import controls and nationalisation. Their leverage is economic, through credit, merchandise and connections across the Indian Ocean, rather than numbers, and they court whichever government holds power.

9.name: Khoja Jamaat
9.text:
A small congregation of Khoja Twelver Shia merchants from Gujarat and Bombay keeps a prayer hall in Colombo and follows the leading clerics of Najaf, above all Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim. Through travelling preachers and pamphlets its members also hear of the exiled Ruhollah Khomeini, who has taught in Najaf since 1965.

Its most devout members want the community guided by the rulings of the clergy, strict observance of Muharram and Islamic law in family matters, and distance from secular politics and Western manners. In Ceylon it has no political organisation; its leverage is limited to the wealth of a few trading families and their ties to Bombay and Karachi.

10.name: All Ceylon Jamiyyathul Ulama
10.text:
The All Ceylon Jamiyyathul Ulama, founded in 1924, is the council of Muslim theologians that speaks for orthodox Sunni Islam among Ceylon's Moors and Malays. It issues religious rulings, guides the madrasas and the sighting of the moon, and works closely with the state through the Muslim members of both main parties.

It counsels loyalty to lawful government, defends Muslim personal law and the Quazi courts, and seeks state support for Muslim schools and the teaching of Arabic. Politically quietist and socially conservative, it draws its leverage from the mosque network and from a community whose votes both the UNP and the SLFP court.

11.name: Khilafat Iyakkam
11.text:
A handful of young Muslims who have studied in Medina, Cairo and Karachi gather in study circles in Colombo, Kattankudy and Beruwala, reading pan-Islamist pamphlets and the writings of Sayyid Qutb, executed in Egypt in 1966. They have no leader of standing and no public face, and their elders keep a wary eye on them.

They reject nationalism, secular parties and the ulama's accommodation with the state, and dream of a single caliphate uniting the Muslim world under the Sharia. In Ceylon they are marginal; their only leverage is the restlessness of educated youth in the Muslim towns and the money and literature that flow from the Gulf.

12.name: Jamaat-e-Islami
12.text:
Jamaat-e-Islami established its Ceylon organisation in 1954, inspired by Abul A'la Maududi and rooted mainly among Tamil-speaking Muslims of Colombo and the east coast. It runs study circles, publications and a youth wing, and works through education and preaching rather than elections.

It aims at an Islamic revival in private and public life, modern schools combining religious and secular learning, and a Muslim community that thinks politically as Muslims rather than as clients of the big parties. Cautious, legalistic and anti-communist, it has leverage among teachers, students and the Muslim towns of the Eastern Province.

13.name: Ceylon Administrative Service
13.text:
The Ceylon Administrative Service replaced the colonial Ceylon Civil Service in 1963 and runs the island's state machinery: the Government Agents and their district kachcheris, and the permanent secretaries of the ministries. Its senior ranks are still English-educated, but a Sinhala-educated generation is rising fast.

It stands for orderly administration, planning, the rice ration and the expanding public corporations, serving each elected government while quietly shaping its policy. Non-aligned by instinct and statist by habit, it is the indispensable executor of every reform, and its leverage grows with each nationalisation, ration book and import licence.

14.name: Sri Lanka Nidahas Pakshaya
14.text:
Founded in 1951 by S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike, the Sri Lanka Freedom Party swept to power in 1956 on a wave of Sinhala Buddhist nationalism and governed again from 1960 to 1965 under his widow, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, the world's first woman prime minister. Now the main opposition, it leads the United Front with the LSSP and the Communists.

It champions non-alignment, a middle path of democratic socialism, Sinhala as the official language, the foremost place of Buddhism, nationalisation of key industries and protection of the rural poor. Its base is the Sinhala-educated village: the monks, ayurvedic physicians, teachers, farmers and workers who were the five great forces of 1956.

15.name: Associated Newspapers of Ceylon Limited
15.text:
Associated Newspapers of Ceylon, known as Lake House after its Colombo headquarters, publishes the Daily News, the Ceylon Observer, Dinamina and Thinakaran and dominates the island's press. Founded by D. R. Wijewardena, it is steered by his family and by Esmond Wickremesinghe, its managing director and a key organiser behind the UNP.

Around Lake House gathers Colombo's propertied elite: the great business families, plantation agency houses, importers and landowners. They want private enterprise, a press free from state control, an end to import rationing and a firm line against the Marxist parties. Their leverage is money and the power to set the national agenda every morning.

16.name: Ceylon Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
Founded in 1839, the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce is the island's oldest business association, long dominated by British agency houses and now increasingly by Ceylonese firms. It speaks for exporters of tea, rubber and coconut, for banks, shippers and importers, and it enjoys easy access to Dudley Senanayake's government.

It campaigns for free trade, relaxation of exchange and import controls, low taxes on enterprise and guarantees for foreign investment, and it welcomed the dual exchange rate scheme of 1968. It fears the United Front's nationalisation programme above all; its leverage lies in its hold on the export economy and the foreign exchange it earns.

17.name: Wildlife and Nature Protection Society
17.text:
Founded in 1894 by planters, naturalists and sportsmen, the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society is one of the oldest conservation bodies in Asia. Its members, civil servants, scientists and hunters turned protectors, campaigned for Yala and Wilpattu national parks and keep watch over the island's elephants, leopards and forests.

It presses for more sanctuaries, stricter wildlife laws, protection of elephants from crop-raiding killings and of forests from clearance for new settlements and irrigation schemes. Small and largely English-speaking, it has influence through its journal, Loris, and through its friends in the Department of Wild Life Conservation.

18.name: Lanka Sama Samaja Pakshaya
18.text:
Founded in 1935, the Lanka Sama Samaja Party was once the strongest Trotskyist party in the world, until the Fourth International expelled it in 1964 for joining Sirimavo Bandaranaike's government. Led by N. M. Perera, Colvin R. de Silva and Leslie Goonewardene, it is now a pillar of the United Front.

It demands nationalisation of banks, plantations and foreign trade, a republican constitution, workers' councils and an independent socialist foreign policy. Its strength lies in Colombo's working class, the Ceylon Federation of Labour, its Western Province strongholds and a brilliant leadership; the price of alliance with the SLFP has been acceptance of Sinhala as the sole official language.

19.name: Communist Party of Ceylon (Peking Wing)
19.text:
The pro-Peking communists broke from the Communist Party of Ceylon in 1963–64 under N. Shanmugathasan, a veteran trade union organiser and the party's general secretary. Rejecting the parliamentary road, the party led militant campaigns against caste oppression in Jaffna in 1966–68, though defections, including that of Rohana Wijeweera, have cost it many young cadres.

It upholds Mao Zedong Thought, condemns Moscow's revisionism and the United Front's reformism, and calls for protracted revolutionary struggle. Its leverage lies in the Ceylon Trade Union Federation, which Shanmugathasan took with him at the split, among Jaffna's oppressed castes and in Peking's moral and material support.

20.name: Mahajana Eksath Peramuna
20.text:
The Mahajana Eksath Peramuna was the coalition that carried S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike to power in 1956; since 1959 it has been the personal party of Philip Gunawardena, the father of Ceylonese Marxism turned Sinhala nationalist. Gunawardena sits in Dudley Senanayake's national government as Minister of Industries and Fisheries, the UNP's most unlikely ally.

It combines socialist economics with a militant defence of Sinhala Only, Sinhala-educated youth and the Buddhist majority against what it calls Tamil and Christian privilege. Its leverage is Gunawardena's oratory and his Avissawella stronghold, and its value to the government is that it splits the Sinhala nationalist vote.

21.name: Jathika Vimukthi Peramuna
21.text:
The Jathika Vimukthi Peramuna is the party of K. M. P. Rajaratna, the most uncompromising Sinhala extremist in Ceylon's parliament, who made his name with violent agitation against concessions to the Tamil language in the late 1950s. With his wife Kusuma Rajaratna he commands a small but fervent following in the Uva hill country.

It preaches Sinhala supremacy: Sinhala alone in every public sphere, the removal of the Indian Tamils, the curbing of Tamil and Christian influence and a strong hand against the Marxists. Contemptuous of compromise and parliamentary bargaining, it thrives on communal fear; its leverage lies in street agitation and frustrated Sinhala youth and petty traders.

22.name: Ceylon Army
22.text:
Raised in 1949 from the colonial Ceylon Defence Force, the Ceylon Army is a small, largely ceremonial force commanded by Major General D. S. Attygalle. Its officer corps, once dominated by English-educated Christians and Burghers, was purged after the 1962 coup attempt, and in 1966 a former commander, Richard Udugama, was arrested over an alleged plot.

It patrols the northern coast against illicit immigration from India, aids the police in emergencies and performs ceremonial duties. Ill-equipped and untested in battle, it is politically cautious, but its senior officers watch the rise of the left and the restless rural youth with growing unease. In a crisis it is the state's last resort.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Ceylon remains a dominion, and Elizabeth II reigns as Queen of Ceylon, represented since 1962 by Governor-General William Gopallawa, a Kandyan aristocrat. The Crown's defenders include much of the English-educated elite, many Burghers and Christians, and Kandyan chiefly families who value continuity with the old order and its ceremonies.

They uphold the Soulbury constitution, appeals to the Privy Council and membership of the Commonwealth under the Crown. The United Front promises a republic and a new constitution drafted by a constituent assembly, so monarchism has become a defence of the existing state; its leverage lies in legal tradition and the habits of the establishment, not in numbers.
